svg.title: OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials
svg.desc: OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials. Machine-to-machine access tokens, with no user involved. Step 1, Ask as itself: The Orders service asks for a token as itself: its own credentials, no user and no browser. Step 2, Token issued: The server authenticates the client, checks its allowed scopes and returns a short-lived token. Step 3, Call and reuse: The service caches the token and reuses it for every API call, renewing shortly before it expires. Step 4, Drop the shared secret: The stored secret gives way to a signed JWT, a client certificate or a workload identity.

g.text: The Orders service asks for a token as itself: its own credentials, no user and no browser.
The server authenticates the client, checks its allowed scopes and returns a short-lived token.
The service caches the token and reuses it for every API call, renewing shortly before it expires.
The stored secret gives way to a signed JWT, a client certificate or a workload identity.

text.class: tiny mono b f-green occ-w occ-key

g.text: Nobody signs in: the service asks as itself.
Confidential clients only: software that can keep a credential to itself.

text.class: tiny mid sb f-orange occ-w occ-sub

g.text: sub is the client itself, not a person
time-lapse: each dot is 100 API calls
new token before the old one ends
The same cached token rides on every call. No token request per call.
Stronger than a stored shared secret:
private_key_jwt · a signed JWT assertion, the one shown here
The client signs a short-lived JWT; the server stores only its public key.
tls_client_auth · a client certificate, mutual TLS
The TLS handshake proves the client holds the certificate’s private key.
workload identity · no stored credential at all
The platform issues a short-lived token, exchanged for an access token.
